title: ACSM Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
findings: Resistance training benefits muscle outcomes; ≥10 sets/muscle/week tended to enhance hypertrophy; heavy loads enhance 1RM; failure and periodization not consistently superior.
limitations: Overview of prior reviews; group tendencies, not personalized thresholds; coding of sets varies.

title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains
findings: Greater weekly training volume generally supports hypertrophy with diminishing returns; fractional indirect-set counting fit dataset best.
limitations: Statistical fractional coefficient is NOT a universal 1S=0.5P physiological constant; correlational dose modeling.

title: Effects of resistance training performed to repetition failure or non-failure on muscular strength and hypertrophy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
findings: No statistically clear overall superiority of momentary failure over nonfailure for strength or hypertrophy.
limitations: Study definitions, volume and populations vary; does not establish best precise RIR.

title: Exploring the Dose-Response Relationship Between Estimated Resistance Training Proximity to Failure, Strength Gain, and Muscle Hypertrophy: A Series of Meta-Regressions
findings: Hypertrophy may improve closer to failure; strength gains occur over wider RIR; exact relationship uncertain.
limitations: RIR retrospectively estimated in constituent studies; not proof that 0 RIR is optimal.

title: Influence of Resistance Training Proximity-to-Failure on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
findings: Momentary muscular failure did not clearly outperform nonfailure in subgroup analysis.
limitations: Outcome depends on operational definitions and evidence base.

title: Effects of Resistance Training Performed to Failure or Not to Failure on Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy, and Power Output: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
findings: When volume equated, failure vs nonfailure did not clearly differ for hypertrophy; context affects apparent results.
limitations: Hypertrophy subset small; cannot support exact 1/0 RIR protocol.

title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: A systematic review and meta-analysis
findings: On average greater weekly set volume linked to greater hypertrophy.
limitations: Older relatively small literature; per-muscle set counting differs across studies.

title: Resistance Training Volume Enhances Muscle Hypertrophy but Not Strength in Trained Men
findings: Higher volumes may provide additional size gains in trained men, not necessarily matching incremental strength gains.
limitations: Specific sample, length and program; cannot be generalized as universally best volume.

title: Muscle hypertrophy and strength gains after resistance training with different volume-matched loads: a systematic review and meta-analysis
findings: Heavier training generally favored maximum strength; hypertrophy outcomes more similar across load ranges.
limitations: Volume-load equivalence not identical to weekly set matching; inclusion protocols vary.

title: How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy? A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining the effects of resistance training frequency
findings: Volume-equated hypertrophy effects largely similar across different weekly frequencies.
limitations: HARDSET 2-exposure rule is organizational, not a biological must.

title: Efficacy of Split Versus Full-Body Resistance Training on Strength and Muscle Growth: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
findings: When volume equated, split vs full-body yielded similar hypertrophy and strength outcomes in reviewed studies.
limitations: Small/moderate evidence base; individual schedules and fatigue still matter.

title: Effect of free-weight vs. machine-based strength training on maximal strength, hypertrophy and jump performance – a systematic review and meta-analysis
findings: No consistent hypertrophy advantage for machines or free weights; strength has task specificity.
limitations: Only subset measured hypertrophy; selection should account for skill/safety.

title: Effects of Periodization on Strength and Muscle Hypertrophy in Volume-Equated Resistance Training Programs: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
findings: Periodization offered strength benefits in reviewed settings; no clear hypertrophy advantage when volume equated.
limitations: Volume equalization, populations and block designs differ.

title: Exercise dosing to retain resistance training adaptations in young and older adults
findings: Young participants preserved many size adaptations at substantially reduced dose; older participants showed different maintenance responses.
limitations: Specific detraining/maintenance scenario; no universal maintenance-minimum sets.

title: Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
findings: Concurrent endurance and strength training did not generally compromise hypertrophy/maximal strength; explosive strength may be attenuated.
limitations: Individual workload and scheduling still important; not a personal tolerance guarantee.

title: Give it a rest: a systematic review with Bayesian meta-analysis on the effect of inter-set rest interval duration on muscle hypertrophy
findings: Rest interval length can influence quality of volume and possibly hypertrophy; a practical rest period should sustain output.
limitations: Does not validate the precise HARDSET 2.5–4 / 1.5–3 min bands for every user.

title: Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations Between Low- vs. High-Load Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
findings: Hypertrophy can develop across loading ranges; heavier loads generally favor maximal dynamic strength.
limitations: Conditions often involved sets to failure; no universal best rep range.

title: Does Muscle Length Influence Regional Hypertrophy? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
findings: Evidence about longer vs shorter mean muscle length suggests small/contextual differences; caution with sweeping claims.
limitations: Studies differ in achieved muscle-length contrasts, muscles and regional measures.

title: Repetitions in Reserve Is a Reliable Tool for Prescribing Resistance Training Load
findings: RIR-based load prescription can be repeatable in tested novice participants and exercises.
limitations: Reliability of load selection is not perfect accuracy of RIR on every rep/exercise.

title: Estimating Repetitions in Reserve for Resistance Exercise: An Analysis of Factors Which Impact on Prediction Accuracy
findings: RIR estimates varied; estimates tended to underestimate actual reserve, and improved closer to failure in tested protocols.
limitations: Small sample and limited lifts/loads; RIR remains an estimate, not objective truth.

title: Muscle Growth Is Very Strongly Correlated with Strength Gains after Lower Body Resistance Training: New Insight from Within-Participant Associations
findings: Within-participant correlations of size and strength gains were strong in one specific lower-body protocol.
limitations: Does not make strength a precise non-imaging estimator of all-muscle hypertrophy.

title: Ultrasound Muscle Thickness Is a Poor Index of Criterion Magnetic Resonance Imaging Measures of Resistance Training-Induced Muscle Growth
findings: Local ultrasound thickness changes did not reliably represent individual MRI changes in quadriceps volume.
limitations: Specific imaging protocol, population and muscle group; not all US applications invalid.

title: Early resistance training-induced increases in muscle cross-sectional area are concomitant with edema-induced muscle swelling
findings: Early apparent increases in muscle cross-sectional area may include edema.
limitations: Small novice study and measurement methodology limit generalization.

title: Effects of Strength Training on Running Economy in Highly Trained Runners: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis of Controlled Trials
findings: Strength training (resistance plus plyometric, 2-3x/week, 8-12 weeks) improved running economy in highly trained middle- and long-distance runners (SMD -1.42).
limitations: Only 5 studies, 93 runners with VO2max >60; wide confidence interval; mostly low-moderate loads combined with jumps and sprints.
verification: PubMed (NCBI E-utilities) metadata, abstract and retraction/erratum notices checked on 2026-11-12

title: Effect of Strength Training Programs in Middle- and Long-Distance Runners' Economy at Different Running Speeds: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
findings: High-load (>=80% 1RM), plyometric and combined strength training improved running economy (small to moderate effects); submaximal-load (40-79% 1RM) and isometric training did not.
limitations: Certainty moderate (low for combined); effects depend on running speed and VO2max; runner populations only.
verification: PubMed (NCBI E-utilities) metadata, abstract and retraction/erratum notices checked on 2026-11-12

title: The Effect of Strength Training Methods on Middle-Distance and Long-Distance Runners' Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
findings: High-load and combined strength training improved running performance (time trial, time to exhaustion); plyometric alone not significant; no method changed VO2max, vVO2max, MMSS or sprint capacity.
limitations: Certainty very low to moderate; heterogeneous protocols and populations.
verification: PubMed (NCBI E-utilities) metadata, abstract and retraction/erratum notices checked on 2026-11-12

title: Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries: a systematic review, qualitative analysis and meta-analysis
findings: Strength-training-based prevention programmes reduced sports injury risk (RR 0.338) in athletes aged 12-40, with a dose-response association.
limitations: Only 6 RCTs, 177 injuries; mixed sports and ages; not specific to runners.
verification: PubMed (NCBI E-utilities) metadata, abstract and retraction/erratum notices checked on 2026-11-12

title: Do Exercise-Based Prevention Programs Reduce Injury in Endurance Runners? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
findings: In endurance runners, exercise-based prevention programmes did not significantly reduce running-related injury risk or rate overall; a post hoc analysis of supervised programmes only showed lower risk.
limitations: 9 RCTs, 1904 participants, 7 of low quality; supervised-only finding is post hoc and may reflect compliance.
verification: PubMed (NCBI E-utilities) metadata, abstract and retraction/erratum notices checked on 2026-11-12

title: Human tendon adaptation in response to mechanical loading: a systematic review and meta-analysis of exercise intervention studies on healthy adults
findings: Achilles and patellar tendons increased stiffness (SMD 0.70), Young's modulus and CSA after >=8-week loading interventions; stiffness adaptation depended on loading intensity, not contraction type.
limitations: Healthy adults 18-50; 264 participants; tendon properties, not injury or running outcomes.
verification: PubMed (NCBI E-utilities) metadata, abstract and retraction/erratum notices checked on 2026-11-12

title: Mechanical, Material and Morphological Adaptations of Healthy Lower Limb Tendons to Mechanical Loading: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
findings: Mechanical loading, mainly resistance training, increased lower-limb tendon stiffness (SMD 0.74) and modulus; higher-strain resistance protocols produced greater adaptation.
limitations: Tendon properties only; does not show reduced injury or better running performance.
verification: PubMed (NCBI E-utilities) metadata, abstract and retraction/erratum notices checked on 2026-11-12
